passage: Kishore, you asked why I never call Vinod. Your uncle Chetan has an old story about that. Sit. When I was fifteen, I thought Vinod had forgotten my birthday. I said nothing. I stopped answering his notes, moved to the back bench and took the other road home. I told myself, if he cares, he will ask. He did ask, once, and I looked at my shoes. Vinod decided I was angry about the science project partner he had picked, which was not it at all. He stopped asking. By Diwali we nodded in the corridor like strangers, and the weeks turned into a habit. Last year, forty years on, I met Vinod at a wedding, and he still believed it was about the science project. I never told him about the birthday.

qa.q: Where did Chetan sit after he stopped answering Vinod's notes?
qa.a: Chetan moved to the back bench.

qa.q: What did Chetan hope for by staying silent, and what feeling sat behind it?
qa.a: Chetan hoped Vinod would notice and ask, feeling hurt and proud about the birthday he thought had been forgotten.

qa.q: What could the young Chetan have done when Vinod asked, and why?
qa.a: Chetan could have said that the birthday hurt, because one honest sentence would have replaced Vinod's wrong guess about the science project.

qa.q: How did Vinod read Chetan's silence?
qa.a: Vinod read it as rejection and guessed it was about the science project partner, so Vinod stopped asking and the distance hardened.

grounding: The student stops replying and sits elsewhere hoping the problem disappears, the friend takes it as rejection and guesses the cause wrongly, and the distance hardens over weeks.
